newsitem.title: USA: MUNI ISSUER FOCUS - Gulf Breeze, Fla., loan pool.
newsitem.headline: MUNI ISSUER FOCUS - Gulf Breeze, Fla., loan pool.

text.p: The northwest Florida City of Gulf Breeze will fund its government loan pool with an inflation-indexed muni issue of $100 million to $160 million.
The deal is expected to price Tuesday via Raymond James & Associates Inc and is only the second in the muni market to link coupon rates to the Consumer Price Index.

"The CPI structure is something we've been looking at a number of months. It's taken a while, obviously, to do the education, not just to educate the issuer, but educate the investors and ourselves," said Raymond James Vice President Charles LeCroy.
"Once everyone understands the program, how these bonds really work and what types of performance these can generate, the demand is definitely there," LeCroy said.

The muni market's first CPI-linked issue was a $40 million City of Orlando, Fla., deal brought to market by Goldman Sachs & Co. It priced at 125 basis points over the six month change in the inflation index and had maturities out to 10 years.

The Gulf Breeze deal will have maturities out to 20 years and is expected to be priced at about 155 basis points over the six month change in the CPI, Peter Delahunt, Raymond James' national sales manager, told Reuters.
"Our target is institutional. We think that in the long run retail will be a substantial player, but it just takes a little bit longer for that process to take," LeCroy said.
The Gulf Breeze pool has made $380 million of loans since it began operating in 1985 and has a long list of potential borrowers throughout the state, LeCroy said.
The new issue will fund floating-rate loans to local governments for capital projects. MBIA Insurance Corp will insure the issue, and has the right to approve the loans.
"This is a CPI-reset bond. It's technically a floater but there's no remarketing component," LeCroy said.

LeCroy said the structure could reduce borrowing costs by 15 to 50 basis points by eliminating the liquidity facility that would traditionally be provided by a bank and another eight to 12.5 basis points by eliminating the remarketing fees to the underwriter.
"If you can eliminate those, you've suddenly created a more attractive program," LeCroy said. "We think it just produces a good transaction, a good rate for the client."

He said the deal also allows borrowers to prepay at par at any time, enabling them to fix an attractive rate but giving them the benefits of a short-term floating investment rate. "The borrowers find it attractive. Its flexibility and terms are very attractive."
Raymond James had previously planned to structure the Gulf Breeze deal with fixed-rate, zero-coupon bonds and a fixed-to-floating interest rate swap.
That structure was abandoned after questions were raised by bond counsel quoted in the financial press.
"No investor wants to buy a deal that has even positive publicity," LeCroy said.
But the firm is still convinced that structure could work.
"We know other underwriters are still exploring that structure, as are we," LeCroy said. "That structure will require further refinement."
Gulf Breeze City Manager Edwin Eddy said he was "very happy" to participate in the new deal.
LeCroy predicted it would be prompt other issuers to pursue similar deals if it succeeds.
"There's no shortage of issuers trying to do these CPI-linked issues if it can save them money," LeCroy said.
